co_black_wall_the.blurb: A high-altitude cliff on the flanks of Mt. Blue Sky, the peak once known as Mount Evans, west of Denver near Idaho Springs. This is committing multi-pitch trad territory at roughly 12,000 to 13,000 feet, with routes that run from a few pitches to well beyond that. Most lines sit in the 5.10 to 5.11 range, with a handful of 5.12 climbs, a single 5.8 and one 5.13 at the top end. The rock is solid, the exposure is real, and storms, wind and sharp temperature swings can arrive in any season. Expect a full rack with big cams for the off-width lines, a long walk-and-rappel entry, and very little company.
co_black_wall_the.approach: Walk north from the lake-side parking, go up and over the hill to the col, then hunt for the rappel anchors along the rim of the cliff. Rope down to the base of the routes; two long ropes are handy. The alternative is to drop from the col and walk along the foot of the wall.

co_trad_lands_the.blurb: A compact, sunny wall on the Golden Cliffs side of North Table Mountain, just outside Golden. Climbs here are short, mostly under 70 feet, and split fairly evenly between gear-protected lines and bolted ones, with a couple of boulder problems and a top-rope option mixed in. Difficulty centres on the 5.7 to 5.10 band, with a few easier lines and one or two harder ones, so it suits newer leaders building mileage as well as people after a quick after-work session. Features include a roof, a chimney and a slab that leads into a crack. Many routes have double-bolt lowering stations, which keeps things simple.

co_non_eggs_the.blurb: A cluster of granite boulders in Alderfer/Three Sisters Park, in the foothills west of Denver near Evergreen, sitting among the problems that make up The Eggs. Nearly all of the climbing here is bouldering, from VB and V0 warm-ups through a solid middle of V3 and V4, with a handful of harder problems up to V8, plus a single top rope and one trad line. It is a good stop for a session when you want variety rather than one big wall. Bring a crash pad; the walk from the trailhead is short and flat to start.

co_nirvana_wall.blurb: A warm, south-western slab in Stanley Canyon, a granite-walled gorge on the Colorado Springs side of the Front Range. The wall mixes slab and crack climbing: roughly equal parts bolted sport lines and gear routes, plus several lines that are set up for top rope. Grades start near 5.4 and run up to the low 5.12s, but most of the climbing sits between 5.7 and 5.10, so there is plenty for newer leaders and for people working mid-grade cracks. Routes are short, around 70 to 90 feet. The walk in is a steady uphill trail followed by a short scramble.

co_j_crack_slab_area.blurb: A section of The Book, one of the big, complex cliffs on Lumpy Ridge above Estes Park. The slab and the boulders beneath it hold mostly traditional climbing, with a few bolted and top-rope lines. Grades run from 5.7 into the 5.12 range, with the bulk in the 5.8 to 5.11 band. Many lines are single pitch, but some of the best known stretch to four or five pitches. Lumpy Ridge generally faces south, which makes for warm days, and afternoon storms are common, so an early start is the habit. Walk in the way you would for the main face of The Book, then branch right to the base.

co_tiara_rado.blurb: A south-facing sandstone cliff band inside Colorado National Monument, beside Grand Junction, on the same ledge system as Liberty Cap. This is a crack-climber's wall: nearly everything is traditional, with offwidths, squeezes and roofs alongside cleaner cracks, and a couple of aid lines. Difficulty is fairly stiff, mostly 5.10 and 5.11 with a few easier and a few harder lines up to the low 5.13s. The monument's soft desert sandstone is best in the cooler half of the year, since summers run hot. Expect a hike of half an hour or more to reach the upper tier.
